facts.claim: "The Few Things (with Charlotte Lawrence)" was released on August 10, 2018 by StarkerSaxeSongs, LLC as a single.
The song was written by JP Saxe and Ryan Marrone.
The duet is a new version of a solo song that Saxe first released in March 2018.
Saxe said the song is the most honest he has been in a love song. He said it comes directly from a conversation, and that the video is that conversation.

Saxe said the song exists because love can be very real and very complicated at the same time. He said the collaboration exists because Charlotte is his favorite, and that making the record together was uncomplicated.
Saxe described Charlotte Lawrence as his friend and said it would be fun for the song to exist as a duet.
The original solo video starred Anthony Ramos and Dina Shihabi. Saxe co-directed it with Shihabi.
The original solo version peaked at #6 on Spotify's Global Viral chart and #5 on the US Viral chart. It reached #2 in Sweden and Switzerland.
Saxe's debut single "Changed" was produced by Ryan Marrone. Marrone also co-wrote "The Few Things". Saxe's later single "A Little Bit Yours" was co-written with producers Marrone and Benjamin Rice.
Saxe is a Toronto-based singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist. His grandfather was the Grammy-winning cellist Janos Starker.

research.lineage: The song sits in confessional, lyric-driven pop and singer-songwriter territory, and press describes Saxe as an R&B-leaning, lyric-obsessed Toronto artist whose writing draws on journaling.

draft:
The first thing **The Few Things** does is apologize, sort of. Its narrator has been told, over and over, that they don't share enough, and the reply comes with a sigh you can almost hear: "I've been hearing that my whole life / I promise, it's not just you." It's a tender line and a defensive one at once. It tells the partner they aren't the problem. It also quietly tells them this isn't going to change. The song never settles which of those it means, and that's why it feels true.

JP Saxe wrote it with Ryan Marrone, the producer behind his debut single "Changed." Saxe has called it the most honest he's been in a love song, and said it came straight out of a conversation. You can hear that origin in the writing. The verses argue the way people do at a kitchen table, half reassurance and half self-justification. When the partner says they feel insecure, the narrator admits to not taking it seriously, which is a startling thing to put in a love song. It's confidence that tips into dismissal, and the very next breath tries to make up for it with an offer to say more. Later comes a plainer confession: the narrator keeps a lot to themselves, but this person is more a part of them than anyone else.

Then the chorus, which does the saying more. The partner becomes one of the few certain things in a life the narrator doesn't narrate out loud, solid enough to build a world on. The real turn is the request underneath it: "And I want you to unravel me." It's a strange kind of romance. Someone who can't open up asks the other person to do the opening, and "come closer, come closer" repeats until it sounds less like an invitation and more like a plea.

The sound stays out of the way. An acoustic guitar is fingerpicked in a steady pattern, a bass holds simple sustained notes, and a soft kick and snare keep a slow, swaying pulse. The vocals are breathy and close, recorded so dry you can hear the air around them. This is the confessional, lyric-first pop Saxe works in, with an R&B lean in the patience of the groove, and the plain production fits a song about saying less than you feel.

Saxe first released it solo in March 2018. This version brings in Charlotte Lawrence, whom he calls his friend and his favorite, and a second voice shadows the lead, often in unison or a close interval. Saxe said the song exists because love can be very real and very complicated at once. Two voices singing a confession meant for one makes that complication easier to hear. The private admission starts to sound like something both people are working through.

It sticks because it gives the quiet partner's side of an old argument, and you feel how much love can sit inside the words someone can't quite say.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote: "I've been hearing that my whole life / I promise, it's not just you"
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly, and it is two consecutive lines.

factCheck.claim: The song opens with / its "first thing" is an apology
factCheck.note: The quoted line is the fourth line of the song, not the first. Reworded to refer to the first verse.

factCheck.claim: The reply comes with a sigh you can almost hear
factCheck.note: No pass describes a sigh. Replaced with the breathy delivery that all three passes agree on.

factCheck.claim: Saxe wrote it with Ryan Marrone, the producer behind his debut single "Changed"
factCheck.note: Marrone co-wrote the song and produced "Changed".

factCheck.claim: Saxe called it the most honest he's been in a love song and said it came straight out of a conversation
factCheck.note: Sourced to the Rock the Pigeon interview.

factCheck.claim: The narrator admits not taking the partner's insecurity seriously and then offers to say more
factCheck.note: Lyrics: "when you say you're insecure about my feelings / I don't take it serious" and "But if you need me to tell you more".

factCheck.claim: The narrator keeps a lot to themselves, but this person is more a part of them than anyone else
Lyric quote: "And I want you to unravel me" and the repeated "come closer, come closer"
factCheck.note: Both are in the lyrics exactly as quoted.

factCheck.claim: Fingerpicked acoustic guitar in a steady pattern
factCheck.note: Passes 1 and 3 agree. Pass 2 says electric, but two passes are enough.

factCheck.claim: A soft kick and snare keep a slow, swaying pulse
factCheck.note: Only pass 2 says "soft" and "swaying", and only passes 2 and 3 name kick and snare. Reworded to light drums with a slow, gentle pulse, which all three passes support.

factCheck.claim: Vocals are breathy and close, recorded so dry you can hear the air around them
factCheck.note: Breathy, close-miked and dry are supported. "Hear the air around them" is an embellishment, so it was removed.

factCheck.claim: An R&B lean in the patience of the groove
factCheck.note: Press calls Saxe R&B-leaning, but nothing in the listening passes places that in the groove.
